messages.subject_clean: About inla.mesh.create.helper
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am using inla-spde approach now. When I used inla.mesh.create.helper to generate triangulation, I found that domain points could make much difference in computing time.
For example,:

 dmp <- matrix(c(-9000,-98000,-9000,98000,480000,98000,480000,-98000),ncol=2,byrow=T)
 mesh <- inla.mesh.create.helper(,dmp,max.edge=c(10000,100000))

it will give result very quickly (no more than 1s).. However, if I make relatively small changes to the domain points, it will take more time, e.g.

 dmp <- matrix(c(-9500,-97000,-9500,97000,470000,97000,470000,-97000),ncol=2,byrow=T)
 mesh <- inla.mesh.create.helper(,dmp,max.edge=c(10000,100000))

Although it is not big problem since the domain points are not quite important for modelling, I am still curious about why this happens.

Cheers,
Ryan

On 1 August 2013 17:24, Liu David <xyli...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I am using inla-spde approach now. When I used inla.mesh.create.helper to
> generate triangulation, I found that domain points could make much
> difference in computing time.

Hi,
you've encountered a known and hard-to-fix bug that throws the meshing
software into an infinite loop in the initial stages of constructing
the triangulation (so it doesn't just take longer time, it essentially
never terminates!).  The bug is typically triggered by very regular
integer inputs, for which the initial convex Delauney triangulation is
non-unique.  The software makes an effort to detect these situations,
but in some cases the detection fails.

One workaround that usually works is to shift the input so that the
points are not in integer coordinates, and then shift the output back:

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(,dmp-0.5,max.edge=c(10000,100000),plot.delay=0,n=c(16,16))
mesh$loc[,1:2] = mesh$loc[,1:2]+0.5

Another workaround is to change the number of points in the domain
extensions.  In your example the following seems to work, for example:

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(,dmp,max.edge=c(10000,100000), n=c(16,16))

If you are on a Linux machine (and perhaps on OSX) you can see what
goes on by specifying plot.delay, for example:

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(,dmp,max.edge=c(10000,100000), plot.delay=1)

This will show the algorithm at work; when it fails to detect
non-uniqueness of the Delauney triangulation it will try "flipping" a
single edge indefinitely.

PS. inla.mesh.2d() is the new name for inla.mesh.create.helper(); the
latter name still exists to support old code.
We're in the process of documenting all these functions...

Finn

On Aug 2, 2013, at 7:11 PM, Liu David <xyli...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Yes, I have seen it and known how to use the spde approach. However, what I want to understand is, which part of the code does the calculation of precision matrix?

The precision matrix is computed as part of the command to make the spde1/spde2 object.  The actual calculation takes place in some C code for speed reasons.

> And for the parameter \alpha, it says that \alpha relates to the smoothness parameter of the process ( "the process" referes to x(u), right?). However, in later calculation, finite element method (FEM) is used to represent x(u) which is of C^0 continuity. How do you assure that x(u) can be more smoother?
>

This is technical.  We strictly speaking perform a minor (but unimportant) "variational crime" by using C^0 basis functions, but everything goes together in the end.  Using higher order regularity would improve the rate of approximation as the mesh is refined, but at a massive computational cost.  There are other solutions (penalty methods, broken FE spaces, etc) which can recover optimal rates but, to be brutally honest, it hasn't really mattered so far.  (Simple tests gave the same results, which is unsurprising from the theory).

For published stuff about this, see the appendices of the original SPDE paper (which shows convergence) and the paper of ours in Volume 1 of Spatial Statistics (which gives rates of convergence of functionals).  I have a bunch of other results sitting around (if you want something specific), but nothing published.

If you want to get some intuition about what happens using lower order FE spaces for higher order problems, any mathetmatical book on finite element methods should give you a lot of information about mixed methods and penalty methods for 4th order elliptic problems, which is pretty much the territory we're wandering around in.

Best wishes,

Dan

As for posterior dependence between the parameters, that _is_ taken into account when evaluating the marginals for the field values, so wether you actually need samples depends, again, on precisely what you are trying to calculate...  That said, you can actually ask inla() to calculate samples with mcmc!

Finn

The FAQ entry

http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-I-want-to-compare-the-results-from-inla-with-those-obtained-with-MCMC-is-there-any-way-to-do-this-using-inla-

gives an example.  Look at the code in the file given by

system.file("demo/Tokyo-compare.R", package="INLA")

for the "magic" parameter you need to specify to get MCMC samples.

> In this case I don't really care what the priors
> are, just as long as they are sensible and suitably vague (but don't
> give ranges bigger than the world etc). If all is done in R-INLA, then
> the between-model consistency issue is automagically solved. Great again!

See the tutorial

http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials/spde-tutorial-from-jss

for how to specify sensible priors when using the default multivariate
normal approach.

> As for the prior specification problem -- which I am loosing interest in
> given the above -- how does this process generate a gamma marginal? If
> you start with correlated log-normals and take a transformation of them,
> then surely the result will be the log-normal multiplied by the jacobian
> of the transormation? Of course, it can be approximated by matching up
> moments/ranges/quantiles(?).

Well, in this case log(sigma^2) and log(kappa) can be used directly in
the specification, so no further transformation is needed.

nu = alpha-dim/2
sigma^2 = gamma(nu)/gamma(alpha)/(4*pi)^nu/kappa^(2*nu)/tau^2

gives

log(tau) =
1/2*log(gamma(nu)/gamma(alpha)/(4*pi)^nu)-log(sigma^2)/2-log(kappa)

so

B.tau = cbind(0.5*log(gamma(nu)/gamma(alpha)/(4*pi)^nu), -1/2, -1)
B.kappa = cbind(0, 0, 1)

gives you the desired parameterisation.  You can then get gamma priors
for sigma^2 and kappa by specifying log-gamma for theta1=log(sigma^2)
and theta2=log(kappa), via

f(..., hyper=list(theta1=list(prior="loggamma", param=...),
theta2=list(prior="loggamma", param=...)))

Note that alpha=2 is the default for inla.spde2.matern (i.e. nu=1 for
dim=2), but nu-values between zero and 1 can be approximated by
specifying a fractional alpha-value, in which case the approximation
discussed in the Authors' response to the JRSSB paper discussion is
used.  Other nu-values are currently not supported.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi all:

My problems which definitely belong to  the Bayesian class is given as follows:
I want to estimate the posterior PDF of parameters of interest, say x1, x2 and x3.
The models are known. Assume y1=x1+x2+x3; y2=x1^2+x2^2+x3^2; y3=x1^3+x2^3+x3^3;
And assume that observations y1, y2 and y3 are normalized distrubtion, specified by u1, v1; u2, v2; and u3, v3, respectively.

Based on the Bayes' thoery:

p(X|D)=(p(D|X)p(X))/p(D)

where p(X|D) is the posterior PDF of parameters x1, x2, x3; p(D|X) is the likelihood function, specified by multivariate normal distribution, Ny1(u1,v1)* Ny2(u2,v2)* Ny3(u3,v3), where Ny1(u1,v1)=1/sqrt(2pi*v1)*exp(-(y1-u1)^2/(2*v1)); p(X) is prior PDF; and p(D) is the normalized factor.

Can INLA handle this problem? If so, can you leave a simple example?

Thanks

Marino David

INLA cannot handle multivariate Normal observations directly except when
the precision matrix is a diagonal. You can however us this trick.
assume

y = mu + b*x + eps

where eps is bivariate normal. then rewrite this as

y = mu + b*x + eps + eps_1

where eps_1 is considered as the observation noise and eps as a 'random
effect'. then prec(eps_1) is fixed and high, wheras 'eps' can be the
iid2d model, a bivariate normal with conjugate prior for the precision
matrix.

Hi,

I've got a similar problem, but I would like to estimate the random walk with drift through a linear combination-specification to obtain the posterior marginal. The reason for this is that later on I will add other latent factors, so I can't get the posterior marginal from the linear predictor.

Below I've attached some sample code that contains my current attempt. In this attempt, the posterior marginal for the random walk with drift is not what I expected, when compared with the marginal of the random walk itself. The marginal of the random walk jumps up and down, but the marginal of the linear combination contains straight lines. The jumps we observe in the marginal of the random walk mode I would expect to observe as well in the marginal of the linear combination. Can some point me to what I'm doing wrong?

Your help is kindly appreciated.

Regards,

Frank van Berkum

___________________________________________________________

require(INLA)

iN    <- 100
x     <- cumsum( rnorm( n=iN, mean= -1, sd=3) )
y    <- x + rnorm( n=iN, mean=0, sd=3 )

# Indices
i.rw <http://i.rw>    <- 1:iN    # random walk part
i.dr    <- 1:iN    # drift part through linear effect

# Formula for random walk with drift
f.rwd    <- y ~ f(i.dr, model="linear", mean.linear = 0, prec.linear=0.1) +
        f(i.rw <http://i.rw>, model="rw1") - 1

# Define data frame
d.rwd    <- data.frame(i.dr=i.dr, i.rw <http://i.rw>=i.rw <http://i.rw>, y=y)

# Linear combination(s) to combine rw and drift
lc.rwd <- inla.make.lincombs(i.dr=i.dr, i.rw <http://i.rw>=rep(1, iN))
# lc.rwd <- inla.make.lincombs(i.dr=i.dr, i.rw <http://i.rw>=i.rw <http://i.rw>)

# Estimate the model
r.rwd <- inla(f.rwd, data=d.rwd, lincomb=lc.rwd, control.inla=list(lincomb.derived.only=TRUE))

# Marginal of linear combination (supposedly random walk with drift)

rwd[,1] <- as.numeric(summary(r.rwd)$lincomb.derived[,"mean"])
rwd[,2] <- as.numeric(summary(r.rwd)$lincomb.derived[,"0.025quant"])
rwd[,3] <- as.numeric(summary(r.rwd)$lincomb.derived[,"0.975quant"])
rwd[,4] <- as.numeric(summary(r.rwd)$lincomb.derived[,"0.5quant"])

rw[,3] <- as.numeric(r.rwd$summary.random$i.rw <http://i.rw>[,"0.975quant"])
rw[,4] <- as.numeric(r.rwd$summary.random$i.rw <http://i.rw>[,"0.5quant"])

If you construct the model so that all the datasets are there, all
effect estimates will use the joint information; the "copy" should be
seen as just an internal technicality, and it truly is the same field in
both parts of the model.
Schematically,
y1 = p1(f(x1))
y2 = p2(f(x2))
x = x1 = x2

One can either estimate the two models separately, and not require
x1=x2, yielding two different x estimates, or specify both models with
the requirement x=x1=x2 in the same inla formula using "copy", in which
case both y1 and y2 will influence the estimate of x.
I _think_ that's essentially what your question is about...

Finn

No. It's a trick to make possible to put a same random
effect on the linear predictor for each likelihood.
So, the information from both dataset is used.
Setting fixed=TRUE (for the copy) you just says that the
random effect entry with same variance on  'both' linear predictor.

A simplest example:

n <- 500
x <- arima.sim(n=n, model=list(ar=0.7))
y1 <- x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.02)
y2 <- x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)

Y <- cbind(c(y1, rep(NA,n)), c(rep(NA,n), y2))

require(INLA)
r <- inla(resp ~ f(i, model='ar1') + f(j, copy='i'),
   data=list(resp=Y, i=c(1:n, rep(NA,n)), j=c(rep(NA,n), 1:n)),
   family=rep('gaussian',2))
r$summary.hy
